summary.simple: Visit the Sun and all eight planets, one after the other.
summary.standard: From the Sun out past Neptune: what is out there, in order.
summary.advanced: From the Sun to the Kuiper belt: the eight planets and what makes each one different.

text.simple: This is our solar system. In the middle is the Sun, a star. Eight planets go round it, and many of them have moons. We live on the third planet: Earth. Let's visit them all!
text.standard: One star, eight planets and hundreds of moons. Everything here circles the Sun, held by its gravity, and all the planets go round it in the same direction, almost in one flat plane. The planets are drawn much bigger than they really are, so you can see them. Let's visit each one, from the inside out.
text.advanced: One star, eight planets and hundreds of known moons, all formed about 4.6 billion years ago from one flattened cloud of gas and dust. That is why the planets orbit in nearly the same plane and in the same direction. Sizes and distances are distorted in this view (see the Scale panel); every fact in the tour uses the true values.

link.simple: Make the Sun a basketball and walk to every planet
link.standard: Shrink the Sun to a basketball and walk the solar system

text.simple: The Sun is a star: a giant ball of glowing hot gas. It is so big that all the planets together would fit inside it. Its light gives us warmth and daylight.
text.standard: The Sun holds 99.8 % of all the mass in the solar system. It is 109 Earths wide, and about 1.3 million Earths would fit inside it. Deep in its core, at 15 million °C, hydrogen fuses into helium. That is where all its light comes from.
text.advanced: A middle-aged, ordinary star: 1.39 million km across, 99.86 % of the solar system's mass. In its core, at about 15 million K, it fuses about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium every second, turning 4 million tonnes of mass into energy (E = mc²). Light leaving its surface reaches Earth 8 minutes 20 seconds later.

text.simple: Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. It has no air to keep it warm. So the day side is hotter than an oven, and the night side is colder than any freezer.
text.standard: The smallest planet, and the fastest: one lap around the Sun takes only 88 days. Mercury has almost no atmosphere to hold heat, so its day side reaches 430 °C while its night side drops to −180 °C.
text.advanced: The innermost planet, 4,879 km across, with a year of 88 days. It turns so slowly that one solar day (sunrise to sunrise) lasts 176 Earth days: two of its years. Without an atmosphere, the surface swings between 430 °C and −180 °C. Its huge iron core fills about 85 % of its radius.

text.simple: Venus is almost as big as Earth, but you could never live there. Thick clouds trap the heat. It is hotter than an oven: the hottest planet of all. It also spins the wrong way round.
text.standard: Venus is nearly Earth's twin in size, but its thick carbon dioxide air traps the Sun's heat: at 465 °C it is hotter than Mercury, although it is twice as far from the Sun. It spins backwards, so slowly that a day on Venus is longer than its year.
text.advanced: 12,104 km across, almost Earth's size. Its atmosphere is 96 % carbon dioxide at 92 times Earth's surface pressure, and a runaway greenhouse effect keeps the surface at 465 °C, day and night. It rotates retrograde in 243 days, longer than its 225-day year; the Sun rises in the west.

text.simple: Home! Earth is the only place where we know there is life. It has water, air to breathe and just the right warmth from the Sun. The Moon goes round it once a month.
text.standard: Our planet is the only world known to have life. It is at just the right distance from the Sun for water to stay liquid, and water covers 71 % of its surface. Its tilted axis gives us the seasons. Watch the flight panel: it tells you how far each trip in this tour really is.
text.advanced: 12,742 km across, 150 million km (1 astronomical unit) from the Sun. Liquid water, a protective magnetic field and an atmosphere of nitrogen and oxygen (made by life itself) make it the only world known to be inhabited. Its axis is tilted 23.4°, which causes the seasons.

text.simple: Mars is red because its dust is rusty. It has the tallest volcano of all the planets. Long ago, rivers flowed there. Today robots drive around on Mars and explore it for us.
text.standard: The red planet gets its colour from iron oxide: rust. Mars is half as wide as Earth and has Olympus Mons, a volcano about 22 km high, two and a half times as tall as Mount Everest. Dry riverbeds show that water once flowed here. Its two small moons are Phobos and Deimos.
text.advanced: 6,779 km across, with a thin carbon dioxide atmosphere at less than 1 % of Earth's pressure. Olympus Mons rises about 22 km; the canyon Valles Marineris is 4,000 km long. Ancient river deltas and lake beds show Mars was once wetter and warmer; water ice remains at its poles and underground. A day lasts about 24 h 40 min, a year 687 days.

text.simple: Jupiter is the biggest planet. All the other planets together would fit inside it! It has no ground to stand on. It is a giant ball of gas, with stripes of clouds and a huge storm called the Great Red Spot.
text.standard: The giant: 11 Earths wide, with more than twice the mass of all the other planets together. Jupiter is made mostly of hydrogen and helium, with no solid surface. The Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has been raging for well over 150 years. Its four big moons were discovered by Galileo in 1610.
text.advanced: 139,820 km across and 318 Earth masses: 2.5 times all the other planets combined. It spins in under 10 hours, which flattens it visibly and stretches its clouds into bands. The Great Red Spot, an anticyclone wider than Earth, has been observed since at least 1831. Ganymede, the largest moon in the solar system, is bigger than Mercury.

text.simple: Saturn has the most beautiful rings. They are made of lots and lots of pieces of ice. Some are as small as sand, some as big as a house. Saturn is so light that it would float in a giant bathtub!
text.standard: Saturn's rings are made of countless chunks of water ice. They are about 280,000 km across but mostly only about 10 m thick. Saturn is 9 Earths wide, yet it is the only planet less dense than water. Its moon Titan is bigger than the planet Mercury.
text.advanced: 116,460 km across, with a mean density of 0.69 g/cm³, less than water. Its main rings span about 280,000 km yet are typically only about 10 m thick: mostly water ice, in pieces from dust to house-sized. They may be far younger than Saturn itself. Of its many moons, Titan has a thick atmosphere and Enceladus sprays an ocean into space.

text.simple: Uranus rolls around the Sun on its side, like a ball rolling along. Something very big may have knocked it over long ago. It is very, very cold.
text.standard: Uranus is tipped over: its axis lies almost flat in its orbit. Look at how its moons circle it, top to bottom. One year on Uranus lasts 84 Earth years, so each pole gets 42 years of sunlight and then 42 years of darkness. It was the first planet found with a telescope, in 1781.
text.advanced: An ice giant 50,724 km across, with its spin axis tilted 98°, probably by a giant impact early in its history. Its moons and rings orbit in its tilted equator plane. Over its 84-year orbit each pole spends about 42 years in continuous daylight. Discovered by William Herschel in 1781, the first planet found with a telescope.

text.simple: Neptune is the farthest planet. Sunlight needs about 4 hours to get there. It has the fastest winds of all the planets. People found it by doing sums, before anyone saw it!
text.standard: The outermost planet, 4.5 billion km from the Sun. A year here lasts 165 Earth years. Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system, up to 2,100 km/h. It was found in 1846 by calculation: astronomers noticed Uranus being pulled off course and worked out where the unseen planet had to be.
text.advanced: 30 AU from the Sun, where sunlight is 900 times weaker than at Earth. Its winds reach about 2,100 km/h. In 1846 Johann Galle found it within 1° of the position Urbain Le Verrier had computed from the irregularities in Uranus's orbit: the first planet discovered by mathematics. Its big moon Triton orbits backwards, probably a captured Kuiper belt object.

text.simple: The solar system does not end at Neptune. Farther out there are icy worlds like Pluto. The space probe Voyager 1 has been flying since your grandparents were young. Now it is the farthest thing people have ever made.
text.standard: Past Neptune lies the Kuiper belt, a ring of icy bodies that includes the dwarf planet Pluto. Much further out, the Oort cloud of comets may reach a third of the way to the next star. Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is more than 25 billion km away: around the end of 2026 its radio signal needs a whole day to reach us.
text.advanced: Beyond 30 AU the Kuiper belt (about 30 to 50 AU) holds icy remnants of the planets' formation, among them Pluto. The Oort cloud of comets may extend beyond 100,000 AU. Voyager 1, launched in 1977, left the Sun's heliosphere in 2012 and passes one light-day from Earth around the end of 2026. The nearest star, Proxima Centauri, is 4.2 light-years away.

summary.simple: Find out how tiny the planets are and how far apart they really are.
summary.standard: The scale lesson: every picture of the solar system lies. See the truth, and feel how empty space is.
summary.advanced: From the usual distorted picture to true scale: sizes, distances, light travel time, and the emptiness in between.

text.simple: This is how the solar system looks in books. But it is not true! The planets are drawn much too big and much too close together. Let's find out what it is really like.
text.standard: This is how the solar system is usually drawn, in books and here too. It is a lie, and a necessary one: the planets are drawn about 10 times too big and far too close to the Sun, or you could not see them at all. This tour takes the lie apart.
text.advanced: This view (Everything visible) is a deliberate distortion: planet sizes are enlarged tenfold and more, and distances are compressed so that all eight orbits fit on one screen. Every textbook diagram does the same. In this tour we remove the distortions one by one.

text.simple: Earth is really big for us. To fly all the way around it in a plane, you would need almost two whole days without stopping.
text.standard: Earth is 12,742 km across and 40,000 km around. A plane flying non-stop around it would need almost two days. Hold on to that feeling of "big": we are going to need it.
text.advanced: 12,742 km in diameter, 40,075 km around the equator: about 45 hours non-stop for an airliner at 900 km/h. Everything that follows is measured against this.

title.advanced: Earth and Moon at true scale

text.simple: Now we switch to the true size! Look how far away the Moon really is. You could put 30 Earths in a row between Earth and the Moon. Astronauts needed three days to fly there.
text.standard: Now we switch to true scale: watch the Moon drift out. It is 384,400 km away, far enough to line up 30 Earths in the gap, or even all the other planets side by side. The Apollo astronauts needed three days to cross it.
text.advanced: True scale from here on. The mean Earth–Moon distance is 384,400 km: 30 Earth diameters, and more than the diameters of the other seven planets added up (about 380,000 km). The Apollo crews took about three days to cross it. The Moon is 3,474 km across, just over a quarter of Earth.

text.simple: Here is the Sun at its real size. If Earth were an orange, the Sun would be as tall as a house! If the Sun were hollow, all the planets together would fit inside it, with lots of room left over.
text.standard: The Sun is 1.4 million km across: 109 Earths side by side. By volume, about 1.3 million Earths would fit inside it. The whole Earth–Moon system you just saw would fit inside the Sun with room to spare.
text.advanced: Diameter 1.39 million km, 109 Earth diameters; volume 1.3 million Earths. The Moon's entire orbit (768,800 km across) would fit inside the Sun, with more than half a million km to spare. It still holds 99.86 % of the solar system's mass.

text.simple: Can you find Earth? The circle only shows where it is. The real Earth is far too small to see from here. A car driving to the Sun without ever stopping would need longer than two long human lives!
text.standard: Earth is 150 million km from the Sun: 11,700 Earths in a row. At this true scale it is far too small to see; the dot and the ring only show where it is. A car at 100 km/h would need 171 years to get there. Sunlight makes it in 8 minutes 20 seconds.
text.advanced: 1 AU = 149.6 million km, 11,740 Earth diameters. The drawn dot is only a marker: Earth's true disc here is a tiny fraction of a pixel. By car at 100 km/h: 171 years; by airliner: 19 years; by light: 499 seconds. Every time you see the Sun, you see it as it was 8 minutes ago.

text.simple: Here are all the planets, at their real distances. The planets near the Sun crowd close together, and the others are very far apart. Sunlight needs about four hours to reach Neptune.
text.standard: The whole planetary system at true scale. Neptune is 30 times as far from the Sun as Earth: 4.5 billion km. Sunlight, the fastest thing there is, needs over 4 hours to get there. The four inner planets huddle in the middle; you can hardly tell them apart.
text.advanced: Neptune's orbit, 30 AU (4.5 billion km) in radius. Light takes 4.2 hours to cross it. The spacing is very uneven: the four rocky planets all fit within 1.5 AU, then comes a wide gap to Jupiter at 5.2 AU, and each giant is 1.5 to 2 times as far out as the one before.

text.simple: Now we switch off the dots and the names. This is how the solar system really looks. The Sun is a tiny dot, and the planets are much too small to see. Space is almost completely empty!
text.standard: The markers and names are off now. This is what is really there: a small Sun and, as far as your eye can tell, nothing else. The Sun and all the planets together fill less than one hundred-billionth of the space inside Neptune's orbit. Space is almost perfectly empty.
text.advanced: Markers and labels off: at true scale no planet covers even a single pixel here. The Sun and the planets occupy less than 10⁻¹¹ of the volume of a sphere with Neptune's orbit as its radius. That emptiness, not the size of the objects, is the real lesson of scale.

title.simple: If the Sun were a basketball
title.standard: If the Sun were a basketball

text.simple: Imagine the Sun as a basketball. Then Earth is a pinhead 26 metres away. Jupiter is a cherry more than a football pitch away. Neptune is a pea more than 7 football pitches away. And the next star? It would be so far away that a plane would need about 8 hours to fly there!
text.standard: Shrink it all so the Sun is a basketball: Earth becomes a pinhead 26 m away, Jupiter a cherry 134 m away, Neptune a pea 776 m away. At that scale the nearest star, Proxima Centauri, is 6,900 km away. You can walk this model on your school field.
text.advanced: At a scale of 1 : 5.8 billion the Sun is a 24 cm basketball, Earth a 2.2 mm pinhead at 26 m, Jupiter 24 mm at 134 m and Neptune 8.5 mm at 776 m. Proxima Centauri, 4.2 light-years away, would be 6,900 km off: the solar system is a tiny island in an ocean of nothing.

title.standard: How do we know the Earth moves?
title.advanced: How do we know the Earth moves?

summary.simple: Sometimes Mars seems to walk backwards in the sky. Find out why!
summary.standard: Mars sometimes loops backwards in our sky. The explanation took two thousand years to settle.
summary.advanced: Retrograde motion, epicycles and the Copernican revolution, from Aristarchus to Bessel.

text.simple: Long ago, people saw that some stars move across the sky. They called them wanderers. Mars usually moves one way, but sometimes it stops and goes backwards for a while. Why? Let's find out.
text.standard: People have watched the sky for thousands of years. Most stars keep their places, but a few wander: the ancient Greeks called them "planetes", wanderers. Mars usually drifts eastwards against the stars, but every two years or so it stops, goes backwards for two to three months, and then carries on. Here is October 2024, just before it happened.
text.advanced: Babylonian astronomers recorded planetary positions for centuries, and the Greeks named the wandering lights "planetes". Mars normally moves eastwards against the stars, but around every opposition (every 780 days) it turns west for 60 to 80 days: retrograde motion. Here is 1 October 2024, two months before the 2024/25 retrograde loop.

text.simple: Now we hold the Earth still, just like it feels to us. Watch the orange line of Mars. It goes forwards, slows down, makes a loop backwards, and then goes forwards again!
text.standard: We now hold Earth still, the way it feels to stand on it, and let time run at a week per second. Watch Mars's orange trail: it moves along, slows down, turns back in a loop and then continues. This is exactly what people saw in the sky from December 2024 to February 2025.
text.advanced: Now the frame of reference is Earth's (non-rotating, fixed to the stars). Mars's trail relative to Earth shows the loop the sky showed: stationary on 7 December 2024, retrograde until 24 February 2025. The Sun also circles Earth once a year in this frame, which is exactly how it appears to us.

text.simple: Stop! On this day, Earth, the Sun and Mars were in a line. Mars was bright and easy to see all night. Right now it looks as if it moves backwards. Look at the small map to see why.
text.standard: Time is paused on the day of opposition: Earth sits right between the Sun and Mars. Mars is at its brightest and in the middle of its backwards loop. The small map beside the scene shows the same moment from above the Sun. Can you see why Mars seems to go backwards?
text.advanced: At opposition Earth lies between the Sun and Mars, and Mars is at the midpoint of its retrograde arc. Closest approach was four days earlier, at 96 million km. The inset shows the same instant heliocentrically: our line of sight to Mars is sweeping backwards because Earth moves faster along its orbit.

title.standard: The old answer: circles on circles

text.simple: Long ago, people thought everything went round the Earth. To explain the loops, they said the planets move on small circles that ride on big circles. It worked quite well, but it was very complicated.
text.standard: If Earth stands still, every planet draws loops, and the Sun circles us once a year. Around 150 AD, Ptolemy explained the loops with circles riding on circles: epicycles. His model predicted the planets well enough to be used for 1,400 years, but it needed more and more circles to stay accurate.
text.advanced: With Earth fixed, Mercury and Venus trace looping rosettes and Mars loops at every opposition. Ptolemy's Almagest (about 150 AD) reproduced this with each planet on an epicycle whose centre moves on a deferent around Earth, plus equants. It was accurate enough to survive 1,400 years, yet it could not explain why the loops of Mercury and Venus stay tied to the Sun.

title.simple: Put the Sun in the middle
title.standard: Copernicus: the Sun in the middle

text.simple: Now we put the Sun in the middle again and watch the same months. No more loops! Earth is on the inside track and runs faster. When it overtakes Mars, Mars only looks like it goes backwards.
text.standard: Back to the Sun in the middle, replaying the same months. The loops are gone: every planet simply circles the Sun. Earth, on the inside lane, is faster and overtakes Mars, and while it passes, Mars seems to slip backwards, like a slower car you overtake on the motorway. Nicolaus Copernicus published this idea in 1543.
text.advanced: The same interval, heliocentric. Retrograde motion is a projection effect: Earth, with the shorter and faster orbit, overtakes Mars, and the line of sight between them swings backwards against the stars. Copernicus (1543) derived the planets' order and relative distances from exactly this. Aristarchus of Samos had proposed a Sun-centred system around 270 BC.

text.simple: Long, long ago, Galileo looked at Jupiter through his new telescope. He saw four small moons going round it. So not everything goes round the Earth! This helped people believe the new idea.
text.standard: We have travelled back to January 1610. Galileo turned his new telescope to Jupiter and found four moons circling it: proof that not everything goes round Earth. He also saw Venus show a full set of phases, like our Moon. That is only possible if Venus goes round the Sun.
text.advanced: January 1610: Galileo discovers Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, a miniature system with a centre other than Earth. Later that year he observes the full cycle of Venus's phases, including gibbous phases that Ptolemy's arrangement cannot produce. It refuted Ptolemy, though not yet Tycho Brahe's hybrid model.

text.simple: Today we know for sure: Earth races round the Sun once a year. In just one second, it goes about as far as you could walk in a whole day! It took people a very, very long time to be completely sure. Spacecraft use this knowledge to fly to other planets.
text.standard: Earth races around the Sun at about 30 km every second. The final proof came in 1838, when Friedrich Bessel measured a nearby star shifting back and forth over the year: the view from a moving Earth. From Aristarchus's first idea to Bessel took more than two thousand years. Every probe we send to Mars relies on it.
text.advanced: Direct proof of Earth's motion came from James Bradley's aberration of starlight (1729) and Friedrich Bessel's parallax of 61 Cygni (1838), 0.3 arcseconds: the stars' apparent shift as Earth moves 300 million km across its orbit. Earth's orbital speed is 29.8 km/s. Kepler's ellipses (1609) and Newton's gravity (1687) turned the picture into physics.

summary.simple: Visit the places where scientists hope to find living things.
summary.standard: Earth, Mars and three ocean moons: the places where we are searching for life.
summary.advanced: Liquid water, energy and chemistry: the most promising places in the solar system to search for life.

text.simple: Every living thing on Earth needs water. It also needs food or sunlight to keep going. Living things are found in amazing places: in ice, in boiling hot springs and deep in the dark sea.
text.standard: All life we know needs three things: liquid water, a source of energy, and the right chemistry, based on carbon. On Earth life turns up almost wherever those meet: in Antarctic ice, in boiling hot springs, and around hot vents on the dark sea floor. So where else in the solar system do they meet?
text.advanced: Life as we know it requires liquid water as a solvent, an energy source (light or chemical gradients) and carbon-based chemistry with elements such as nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur. Extremophiles thrive from −20 °C brines to hydrothermal vents above 120 °C, some with no sunlight at all. That widens the search far beyond Earth-like planets.

title.simple: Mars: a wet planet long ago

text.simple: Today Mars is cold and dry. But long ago it had rivers and lakes. Maybe tiny living things lived there. A robot car called Perseverance is collecting rocks from an old lake to look for clues.
text.standard: Mars is cold and dry today, with air far too thin for liquid water to last. But billions of years ago rivers filled lakes here. Since 2021 the rover Perseverance has been exploring Jezero crater, an old lake bed, and collecting rock samples. Some show patterns that on Earth are often made by microbes; only a lab on Earth can tell for sure.
text.advanced: About 3.5 billion years ago Mars had rivers, deltas and lakes. Perseverance, in Jezero crater since 2021, has cached samples of the old lake deposits; one rock found in 2024 shows mineral patterns that on Earth are often associated with microbes but could also form without life. Water ice survives at the poles and underground.

title.simple: Europa: an ocean under the ice

text.simple: This moon of Jupiter is covered with ice. Under the ice there is a huge ocean of salty water. It holds more water than all the seas on Earth together! A spacecraft is on its way there.
text.standard: Europa, one of Jupiter's big moons, is covered by an ice shell many kilometres thick. Underneath lies a salty ocean holding about twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans. Jupiter's tides knead the moon and keep it warm inside. NASA's Europa Clipper, launched in 2024, arrives in 2030.
text.advanced: Galileo spacecraft magnetometer data revealed a conducting, salty ocean under an ice shell perhaps 15–25 km thick, with about twice the water of Earth's oceans. Tidal flexing by Jupiter provides the heat, and the ocean floor may be in contact with rock, as around hydrothermal vents on Earth. Europa Clipper (launched 2024) arrives in 2030.

text.simple: Enceladus is a small moon of Saturn. At its south pole, fountains of water shoot out into space! The water comes from an ocean hidden under the ice.
text.standard: Enceladus is a small moon of Saturn, only 500 km across. From cracks near its south pole, geysers blast water from a hidden ocean into space. The Cassini spacecraft flew right through them and found salt, organic molecules and hydrogen: the kind of chemistry that microbes on Earth live on.
text.advanced: Only 504 km across, yet geologically active: plumes from the "tiger stripe" fractures at its south pole vent water from a global subsurface ocean. Cassini sampled them directly and detected salts, silica grains that point to hydrothermal activity, molecular hydrogen, organic compounds and, later, phosphates: nearly every ingredient life needs.

title.standard: Titan: a strange twin of Earth

text.simple: Titan is Saturn's biggest moon. It has thick air, clouds, rain and lakes, just like Earth. But it is so cold there that the rain and the lakes are not water!
text.standard: Saturn's largest moon has a thick orange atmosphere, clouds, rain, rivers and lakes, like Earth. But at −179 °C the rain and lakes are liquid methane, not water. There may also be a water ocean deep below the surface. A flying drone called Dragonfly is planned to land there in 2034.
text.advanced: Titan has a nitrogen atmosphere 1.5 times Earth's surface pressure and a methane cycle with clouds, rain and hydrocarbon seas such as Kraken Mare at −179 °C. It may host exotic chemistry in its seas and a water ocean beneath the ice crust. NASA's Dragonfly rotorcraft is to launch in 2028 and land in 2034.

title.simple: Not too hot, not too cold

text.simple: Earth is in just the right place: not too hot like Venus and not too cold like Mars. But the ocean moons show that life might also hide far from the Sun, kept warm from inside.
text.standard: Earth orbits in the "Goldilocks zone": not too hot, not too cold, so water can stay liquid on its surface. Venus is too hot, Mars too cold. But Europa and Enceladus show that oceans can also exist far from the Sun, heated from the inside. The best places to look for life may be under the ice.
text.advanced: The classical habitable zone, where surface water can stay liquid, spans roughly 0.95 to 1.7 AU for the Sun, depending on the climate model. The ocean moons break that rule: tidal heating keeps water liquid under ice at 5 and 9.5 AU. The same idea guides the search for life around other stars.
